title: Scams, Deception & Social Engineering
description: Explore time pressure and cognitive overload through dialogue, evidence and psychological reasoning.

lessons.title: The deadline that isn't yours
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of time pressure and cognitive overload.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre, suspicious messages and social engineering guidance.
nodes.scenario: Alex receives a delivery text saying a parcel will be returned unless a small fee is paid within fifteen minutes.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: This text says my parcel is going back tonight.

turns.speaker: a

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Have you checked the order outside the message?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Not yet. I feel like waiting means I'll lose it.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: The deadline may be making verification seem riskier than paying.

nodes.prompt: Which two statements most directly support the working explanation?
nodes.explanation: The most informative lines reveal what the situation means to the speaker. They suggest that the imposed deadline may be discouraging independent verification before a payment. Other remarks establish circumstances, which can matter without revealing a psychological process.

nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
Social engineering can change the conditions under which someone decides. Time pressure makes caution seem expensive, while a small fee lowers the apparent cost of compliance. The safer test is to leave the supplied link and verify through a trusted, independently accessed channel.

Some real services do have deadlines. Urgency alone justifies verification; it does not prove fraud.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre, suspicious messages and social engineering guidance.

nodes.title: Try a different response
nodes.prompt: The goal is to improve the situation without pretending that you can read the person's mind.
nodes.explanation: A proportionate response deals with the actual situation: Close the text and open the retailer or courier's own site or app to check the order. Its value does not depend on the other person accepting an interpretation of their motives.
nodes.counterexample: Some situations require independent support or safer channels rather than another direct conversation. Some real services do have deadlines. Urgency alone justifies verification; it does not prove fraud.

nodes.title: Repair an overclaim

nodes.explanation: A functional hypothesis identifies what may make a behaviour more likely. It remains open to disconfirmation. Some real services do have deadlines. Urgency alone justifies verification; it does not prove fraud.

nodes.title: New evidence, new judgement
nodes.prompt: What should happen to your working explanation now?

nodes.title: Two people, different meanings
nodes.prompt: Which conclusion accounts for both perspectives without confusing an interpretation with a fact?
nodes.explanation: Each character can be responding to a different meaning of the same event. The immediate issue is still observable. Understanding both viewpoints helps explain the conflict without requiring both interpretations to be equally accurate.
nodes.counterexample: Some real services do have deadlines. Urgency alone justifies verification; it does not prove fraud.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre, suspicious messages and social engineering guidance.

nodes.explanation: A strong test looks for observations that would discriminate between explanations. A courier may genuinely have a time-sensitive delivery problem. If independent evidence favours that account, the formulation should change.
